title: The book found (2 Kings 22)
hook: a lost scroll is found in the Temple, and the prophetess Huldah is consulted

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah told a weeping king that his tears were seen. Your line was the weeping was part of the prayer. Today, a few kings later, the high priest finds something in a Temple under repair.
screen: `THE WEEPING WAS PART OF THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Dust, scaffolding, money changing hands. King Josiah has sent his scribe, Shaphan, to the Temple to sort out payment for the carpenters, builders and masons doing repairs. It's a building job. Then the high priest, Hilkiah, hands the scribe something and says: "I have found the book of the Law in the house of the LORD." He calls it the book of the Law, found inside the house of the Lord itself.
screen: `A TEMPLE UNDER REPAIR.` → `A SCROLL IN THE HOUSE.` → `I HAVE FOUND THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Shaphan reads it and carries it to the king. He gives his report on the builders first, then, almost in passing, mentions the scroll and reads it aloud. When Josiah hears the words of the book, he tears his clothes, and gives his reason in his own words: our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book. So he does something careful. He doesn't act alone on his first reaction. He sends the high priest, the scribe and others to inquire of the Lord, and they go to a woman: Huldah the prophetess, who lives in Jerusalem. The text gives her almost no introduction, only her husband's family and where she lives. Then it gives her the floor. Her answer has two parts. The hard part: the trouble the book describes will come. The tender part is for Josiah himself: because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself when you heard, and tore your clothes and wept, I have heard you. You'll be gathered to your grave in peace. What was the scroll? The text just calls it the book of the law. Some readers suggest it was Deuteronomy, or part of it, and the text doesn't settle the question. What it shows is the moment of finding. A people had the words in their own house and had lost track of them. In the story, the find works less like a treasure than like a mirror. And instead of filing it away, the king listened, wept, asked a prophet, and took it seriously.
screen: `SHAPHAN READS IT TO THE KING.` · `JOSIAH TEARS HIS CLOTHES.` · then, large: `ASK HULDAH THE PROPHETESS.` · then: `THE BOOK AS A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open, as if holding a page, and think of words you already own but haven't read in a long time: a psalm, a prayer from childhood, a blessing on a wall, a letter from a grandparent. Say a few of its words slowly in your head, and ask what they ask of you now that you'd forgotten. If you pray, you can hold those words before God.
Huldah, the prophetess King Josiah sent his officials to when the long-lost book of the law was found and read to him.
Your line: a mirror, not a treasure. The words were in the house all along. Seven hundred eighty days now.

howItsDone: Jews read the finding of the book as part of the book of Kings, and Huldah is remembered in Jewish tradition among the prophetesses of Israel.

chat.says: When Josiah's people found that old scroll, what did the king do?
options: He tore his clothes, then sent to Huldah the prophetess to ask what it meant.
He had it filed away safely, since it was only an old copy.
He read it once, then went straight back to repairing the Temple.
chat.meaning: Hearing the book, Josiah tore his clothes and sent his officials to Huldah, who answered with hard news and a tender word for him.

Josiah.meaning: the king of Judah when the book was found

Shaphan.meaning: King Josiah's scribe, who read the scroll to him

Hilkiah.meaning: the high priest who found the book of the Law

Huldah.meaning: the prophetess in Jerusalem the king's officials consulted

Deuteronomy.meaning: the fifth book of the Torah

sources.quoted: I have found the book of the Law in the house of the LORD.

notes: Quotation is KJV; JPS 1917 believed to read 'the book of the Law' — verify and consider citing JPS.
The suggestion that the scroll was Deuteronomy is phrased as 'some readers suggest'; Keeper may prefer a rabbinic view instead or to cut it.
'Huldah is remembered in Jewish tradition among the prophetesses of Israel' (Talmud Megillah 14a lists prophetesses) — Keeper may want to confirm or cite.
Huldah's words to Josiah (22:19–20) are paraphrased.

Editor: fixed review (the high priest, not workers, finds the scroll); cut the hook's unsupported claim that the book had lain there unread; untangled a garbled sentence about Shaphan's report; replaced speculation about Josiah's motive with his stated reason (22:13); Huldah's introduction gives her husband's family, not only his name.

Audit: 22:8 quotation now JPS 1917 ('the book of the Law'); hook no longer asserts 'not a new book' as fact, only that Hilkiah calls it the book of the Law; 'it felt like a mirror' recast as the story's image rather than a claim about feelings; varied practice opener.
